Subject: TTFT & streaming SLOs — post-call next steps

Hi Sam / Priya —

Thanks again for the demo this morning — great discussion and appreciate the clarity on the primary UX flows. Per our call, I wanted to recap the performance/SL0 items we agreed to validate and propose next steps for a short qualification run. Attaching the template (acme_perf_requirements.xlsx) you can fill if that helps.

Recap of your stated targets:
- TTFT (time-to-first-token): <= 120 ms p95 for short queries (search/autocomplete flow)
- Sustained throughput: peak ~200 qps, burst to 500 qps for non-streaming requests
- Streaming sessions: ~200 concurrent active streams (peaks 400) for chat/assistant experience
- Chunk/cadence: prefer WebSocket, target ~200–300 ms per chunk (small chunks for progressive render)
- Avg response: ~120 tokens, max ~1024 tokens

Questions / items we need from you to size the run: 
1) Traffic shape: expected p95 request size and average request payload (tokens/characters) — if you can share 5–10 sample prompts that would be ideal.
2) Are you OK with an initial qualification on our Hosted environment, or do you want Redwood Dedicated reserved capacity (recommended for stricter TTFT guarantees)?
3) Any constraints on SSE vs WebSocket? You mentioned WebSocket preference — is SSE acceptable as fallback?

Next steps I propose:
- You share the sample prompts + a filled perf template (acme_perf_requirements.xlsx) by end of week.
- We schedule a 60-min technical deep dive (Vivek + SE) to align on run config and metrics to capture.
- Redwood will provide a short SLO proposal and a 1-hour smoke/perf run plan.

I attached the perf template for your convenience. Happy to move faster if you can share the sample payloads now.

Best,
Marissa

Marissa —

Thanks for the clear recap. Confirming answers inline: 

- TTFT: Our internal UX team is shooting for <=120ms p95 for the quick autocomplete/search experience. For longer assistant flows we can tolerate up to 300ms p95 first-byte as long as chunks start streaming quickly.
- Traffic: Typical daily peak ~200 qps, but we plan for bursts to 500 qps during promos. For streaming, we estimate 200 concurrent streams with spikes to ~400.
- Chunk cadence: We prefer WebSocket (bidirectional), but SSE is acceptable if you support the desired cadence. Target cadence ~250 ms average, with payloads of ~50–150 tokens per chunk depending on response.
- Payloads: avg response ~120 tokens, typical prompt lengths ~30–80 tokens; max response size 1024 tokens.

Questions from our side: 
1) How does Redwood’s batching affect TTFT? We need to understand whether enabling automatic batching will add tail latency and if you can disable cross-request batching for low-latency paths.
2) What are per-GPU throughput expectations for the model flavors you recommended? (we're currently modeling costs)

We can do the tech deep dive — Jul 2 at 10:00 AM PT works for our infra lead. I’ll upload a couple of sample prompts and a small trace(1k reqs) tomorrow.

Thanks,
Sam

Subject: Re: TTFT & streaming SLOs — post-call next steps

Sam — great, thanks for the quick answers and for offering the trace/sample prompts. To address your two explicit questions up-front: 

1) Batching and TTFT: our runtime supports both continuous batching and a low-latency path. For strict TTFT targets we can: 
   - Disable cross-request batching for the low-latency route (this reduces GPU efficiency but preserves TTFT).
   - Use very small intra-request micro-batches when needed (size=1–2) to maintain throughput without adding >10–20ms extra to TTFT.
   - Use prefix/KV caching for repeated prompts (autocomplete/search) to reduce work per request.

2) Per-GPU throughput: rough guidance depends on model size and quantization; examples for the family we discussed (opt-13B equivalent quantized): 
   - Non-streaming throughput: ~200–400 token/s depending on sequence length and batch size.
   - Streaming concurrent sessions: a single high-end A100/RTX-class node can sustain ~60–100 concurrent low-latency streams for 1–2k token sessions with strict TTFT if batching is limited.
   - For your target of 200 concurrent streams with headroom to 400, we typically recommend a small dedicated pool (3–6 GPUs) to ensure peak capacity and predictable tail latency.

Proposed qualification plan (short):
- Phase 1 (smoke): 1-hour smoke run on Hosted to validate integration and correct streaming behavior (SSE/WebSocket). Capture p50/p95/p99 TTFT and chunk cadence.
- Phase 2 (load): 2-hour load run using sample trace at 1x and 2x peak traffic to validate tail behavior (p95/p99).
- Observability: we’ll surface per-route token-level latency, chunk cadence histogram, and error rate.

Attachments: I’m including a short SLO proposal (redwood_slo_proposal_v1.pdf) that maps our measurement approach to your stated targets.

Next steps: 
- You upload the sample prompts and the trace (you mentioned tomorrow).
- Confirm whether you prefer Hosted qualification or want us to provision a Dedicated trial (I recommend Dedicated for a production-grade TTFT guarantee).
- Confirm deep-dive Jul 2 10:00 AM PT — we’ll include Vivek (SE) and Rishi (solutions) to walk through config.

If that all looks good I’ll assign a test run and send a lightweight run plan + retention of logs for your compliance team.

Best,
Marissa

Sam / Marissa — quick technical notes ahead of the deep dive so we can focus on the run specifics: 

Key config recommendations for meeting 120ms p95 TTFT with streaming: 
- Transport: WebSocket preferred for client-facing chat (bidirectional). Redwood supports SSE as a fallback; SSE latency characteristics are similar but WebSocket gives slightly lower jitter for small chunk cadence.
- Chunk flush policy: target 200–300 ms flush cadence. We recommend flush-on-token-threshold=16 OR flush-interval=250ms (whichever triggers first) to keep UI responsive.
- Batching: disable cross-request batching for the low-latency route. Keep adaptive micro-batching for non-latency-critical endpoints to preserve efficiency.
- Concurrency per GPU: set logical concurrency cap to 64–96 streams per GPU for 13B-class quantized models. Use a small pool (3 GPUs) to cover 200 concurrent streams with headroom.
- Caching: enable prefix/KV caching for high-duplication autocomplete queries — this often buys 40–60% reduction in per-request work and greatly improves TTFT.
- Monitoring: we will instrument chunk cadence histograms (bucketed 0–50ms, 50–150ms, 150–300ms, 300–600ms), TTFT p50/p95/p99, and per-token generation time.

Run offer: Redwood can provision a 1-hour dedicated smoke run on a small Dedicated pool (3 x A100-equivalent) for a nominal trial fee (or free as part of the POC, pending legal). During that run we will: 
- Capture TTFT p50/p95/p99, per-chunk latency distribution, and GPU utilization.
- Test both WebSocket and SSE endpoints and report recommended chunk policy.

Confirming Jul 2, 10:00 AM PT for the tech deep dive works for me. If you can share the trace and sample prompts ahead of that meeting (even partial), we’ll pre-configure the run and have preliminary expectations ready.

Thanks,
Vivek Kulkarni
